question: On a mortise-view X-ray of the ankle, the medial clear space is 5 mm (upper limit of normal 4 mm) in an isolated lateral malleolus fracture at the level of the syndesmosis. What does this finding imply?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A medial clear space > 4 mm indicates talar subluxation and implies disruption of the deep deltoid ligament. This converts an apparently 'isolated' fibula fracture into an unstable bimalleolar-equivalent injury.

answers.text: Ligamentous medial injury making this a bimalleolar-equivalent fracture requiring ORIF

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Medial clear space > 4 mm indicates deltoid ligament disruption. Even without a medial malleolus fracture, this creates an unstable injury (bimalleolar equivalent) that requires operative fixation of the fibula and assessment of the deltoid/syndesmosis.

answers.text: Isolated posterior malleolus fracture — CT of the ankle is the next step

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The medial clear space widening points to medial ligamentous injury (deltoid disruption), not a posterior malleolus fracture. CT may be used subsequently to assess the posterior malleolus, but the immediate implication is medial instability.
Incorrect. Posterior impingement causes posterior pain and has no bearing on medial clear space. Medial clear space widening indicates talar shift due to deltoid ligament failure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key rule: medial clear space (tibia–talus gap on mortise view) > 4 mm implies deltoid disruption + talar shift. This upgrades any lateral malleolus fracture to an unstable bimalleolar-equivalent, mandating operative fixation.

Well done. Medial clear space > 4 mm = talar subluxation = bimalleolar-equivalent injury. A Weber B fracture with this finding is unstable and requires ORIF regardless of the absence of a medial malleolus fracture.
